overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Merleau-Ponty's clinical arguments. You'll be asked about the phantom limb, the habitual body, grasping vs. pointing, the intentional arc, and the evidential status of the Schneider case.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Merleau-Ponty reject a purely psychological explanation of the phantom limb?

options.html: Because phantom limbs never respond to emotion or memory
options.text: Because phantom limbs never respond to emotion or memory
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Phantoms do respond to emotion and memory. The problem is that they also depend on nerve pathways and have a precise felt posture.

options.html: Because the phantom depends on nerve pathways as well
options.text: Because the phantom depends on nerve pathways as well
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! If the phantom were only a memory or belief, cutting nerve pathways shouldn't abolish it.

options.html: Because psychology can't study bodily experience at all
options.text: Because psychology can't study bodily experience at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The argument is specific: a purely psychological account can't explain the phantom's dependence on nerve pathways.

options.html: Because patients always know their limb is missing
options.text: Because patients always know their limb is missing
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The phantom has an ambivalent presence. The problem for psychology is its dependence on nerve pathways.

forms.stemHtml: Months after a kitchen is rearranged, you still reach for a drawer that has moved. Which of Merleau-Ponty's concepts best describes what's at work?

options.html: The body at this moment, adapting to the new layout
options.text: The body at this moment, adapting to the new layout
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The reach goes to the old place, which reflects the habitual body, not the body at this moment.

options.html: The habitual body, still projecting the old possibilities
options.text: The habitual body, still projecting the old possibilities
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The habitual body keeps open a field of practical possibilities built up over time, even after the situation changes.

options.html: Anosognosia, a refusal to acknowledge the change
options.text: Anosognosia, a refusal to acknowledge the change
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Anosognosia concerns failing to acknowledge an impaired limb. This is the habitual body at work.
Sorry, that's incorrect. The reach is habitual, not performed on command. It reflects the habitual body.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are abstract movements, in Merleau-Ponty's sense? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Pointing to your nose when asked
options.text: Pointing to your nose when asked
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Pointing on command is an abstract movement.

options.html: Moving your arm with no reason to move it
options.text: Moving your arm with no reason to move it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A movement for its own sake requires setting up a virtual situation.

options.html: Imitating a movement someone shows you
options.text: Imitating a movement someone shows you
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Imitation on request is performed outside a practical situation.

options.html: Scratching an itch on your arm
options.text: Scratching an itch on your arm
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Scratching answers to an actual demand. It's a concrete movement.

options.html: Swatting a mosquito on your hand
options.text: Swatting a mosquito on your hand
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Swatting answers to an actual situation. It's a concrete movement.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's term for the pre-reflective projection, around us, of our past, future, human setting, and situation, which unifies perception, action, and understanding? Enter two words.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! In Schneider, Merleau-Ponty says, the intentional arc goes slack.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty calls this the intentional arc.

forms.stemHtml: What is the current status of the Schneider case as evidence?

options.html: It has been fully confirmed by later brain imaging
options.text: It has been fully confirmed by later brain imaging
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Later scholarship has questioned the original reports. Their reliability remains debated.

options.html: It was shown to be invented by Merleau-Ponty
options.text: It was shown to be invented by Merleau-Ponty
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The case comes from Gelb and Goldstein's reports. Its reliability, not its existence, is disputed.

options.html: Its reliability has been questioned and remains debated
options.text: Its reliability has been questioned and remains debated
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Critics raised concerns about repeated testing and later examinations. A careful reader treats it as suggestive evidence.

options.html: It's irrelevant, since Merleau-Ponty never relied on it
options.text: It's irrelevant, since Merleau-Ponty never relied on it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty relied heavily on the case, especially for the intentional arc.

title: Phantom Limbs and the Schneider Case
